senses.gloss:
Datta Tāpasa was hotṛ priest at the snake festival described in the pañcaviṃśa brāhmaṇa.
Foot notes xxv. 15, 3. Cf. Weber, Indische Studien, 1, 35.

Dātyauha, a ‘gallinule,’ is mentioned in the list of victims at the aśvamedha, or horse sacrifice, in the yajurveda. The word is clearly a variant of dātyūha, which occurs in the epics and law books.
Foot notes taittirīya Saṃhitā, v. 5, 17, 1; Maitrāyaṇī Saṃhitā, iii. 14, 6; Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā, xxiv. 25. 39. Pāṇini, vii. 3. 1, derives the word from ditya-vah. Cf. Zimmer, Altindisches Leben, 91.

Dātra (‘cutter’), denoting a ‘sickle,’ is mentioned in the Rigveda. Cows ‘with sickle-shaped marks on their ears’ (dātra-karṇyaḥ) are referred to in the Maitrāyaṇī Saṃhitā. Otherwise the expression is only found later, occurring in the sūtra and epic literature. See also Sṛṇi.
Foot notes viii. 78, 10; nirukta, ii. 1.
iv. 2, 9.
Hopkins, Journal of the American Oriental Society, 17, 86.
Cf. Zimmer, Altindisches Leben, 238.

Dātreya is the patronymic of Arāḍa śaunaka in the vaṃśa brāhmaṇa. Possibly dārteya, ‘descendant of dṛti,’ should be read, but the word may have the same derivation as the latter form with metathesis.
Foot notes Indische Studien, 4, 373.
Cf. St. Petersburg Dictionary, s.v.
